findings.title: Case-sensitive email lookup lets users bypass the block list
findings.body: BlockedEmail.should_block? queries BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first, which is an exact, case-sensitive string match. Email addresses are case-insensitive per RFC 5321, and the User model stores the email as submitted (no downcasing on assignment), so an admin adding `bad@spamclub.com` to blocked_emails will not stop a user signing up with `Bad@SpamClub.com` or `BAD@SPAMCLUB.COM`. Since the entire point of this feature is to reject known-bad addresses, this is a core-functionality bug: the lookup should normalize (downcase and strip) the email before querying, and ideally the BlockedEmail model's uniqueness validation should be made case-insensitive too so admins don't silently end up with duplicate near-spellings.

findings.title: Validator has the side effect of writing to blocked_emails
findings.body: BlockedEmail.should_block? does `record.match_count += 1; record.last_match_at = Time.zone.now; record.save` every time it finds a matching record. It is called from EmailValidator.validate_each, which fires on every User save with `email_changed?` — including profile updates that change an email and any form re-submission that re-validates. As a result match_count and last_match_at are incremented for each validation attempt rather than each actual signup, the validator is no longer idempotent, and a failed DB write inside should_block? raises out of the validator with no rescue (turning a 'blocked email' check into a 500). Statistics should be updated by a separate, explicit call (e.g. in the controller only when the user actually creates an account), and should_block? itself should be a pure check.

findings.title: Read-modify-write race on match_count
findings.body: should_block? loads the record, increments match_count in Ruby, then calls record.save. Two concurrent requests for the same blocked email can each read match_count = N, both increment to N+1, and both save N+1, losing one update. Use an atomic update such as `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all('match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = NOW()')` or `update_counters`.

findings.title: Whitelist/blacklist branches of EmailValidator have no tests
findings.body: The whitelist (SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist) and blacklist (SiteSetting.email_domains_blacklist) branches were moved out of User#email_validator into the new EmailValidator, but the spec only stubs BlockedEmail.should_block?. There is no coverage that an email matching the whitelist passes, that a non-whitelisted email gets the :not_allowed error, that a blacklisted email is rejected, or that an existing whitelist/blacklist error suppresses the blocked-email check. Adding tests for those branches would protect against regressions in the moved logic.

findings.title: Domain-setting regex only escapes dots
findings.body: email_in_restriction_setting? does `setting.gsub('.', '\.')` and feeds the rest directly into Regexp.new. Other regex metacharacters (`*`, `+`, `?`, `|`, `(`, `)`, `[`, `]`, `^`, `$`) in the SiteSetting are interpreted as regex syntax instead of literals, so a value like `mail.ru+` or a multi-domain list with an unexpected separator can match in surprising ways. The legacy code had the same problem, but this is a good opportunity to either escape all regex metacharacters or split the setting on a fixed separator (e.g. `|`) and match each domain literally.
